<reason>B established the decisive distinction between community approval and sufficient cooperation. Its safeguards, livelihood protections, and cancellation criteria supported proceeding despite disagreement without requiring infeasible releases. A raised serious implementation and fairness concerns, but repeatedly assumed that community opposition necessarily destroys cooperation. Its closing then redefined workable cooperation as consent rather than answering B’s distinction. B directly answered the enforcement and compensation questions, while A continued portraying consultation as predetermined despite explicit provisions allowing cancellation. A’s memorable rhetoric made the risks vivid; B supplied the stronger comparative decision rule.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s response to the “consultation is theater” argument was decisive: local evidence can change or cancel a release without objection automatically deciding it. Coupled with the distinction between approval and cooperation, this defeated A’s claim that overriding objections must mean ignoring feasibility.</best_rebuttal>
